title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: In the first days after coming back from Moscow, whenever Levin flinched and flushed, remembering the humiliation of being turned down, he told himself: "This is exactly how I used to flinch and blush, thinking I was completely done for, when I flunked physics and didn't get promoted; and how I thought myself completely ruined after I'd botched that business of my sister's that had been entrusted to me. And yet now, years later, I look back on it and I'm amazed it could have upset me so much. It'll be the same with this trouble. Time will pass, and I won't care about this either."

But three months had gone by and he still hadn't stopped caring about it; it was just as painful to think about as it had been in those first days. He couldn't find any peace, because after dreaming for so long about family life, feeling himself so ready for it, he still wasn't married, and was further from marriage than ever. He was painfully aware, as everyone around him was too, that at his age it isn't good for a man to be alone. He remembered how, before he'd left for Moscow, he'd once told his cowman Nikolay — a simple, good-hearted peasant he liked talking to — "Well, Nikolay, I mean to get married," and how Nikolay had shot back immediately, as if it were a matter beyond any doubt: "And high time too, Konstantin Dmitrievitch." But marriage was now further away than ever. The place was taken, and whenever he tried to picture any of the women he knew stepping into it, he felt it was simply impossible. On top of that, the memory of the rejection, and the part he'd played in it, tormented him with shame. However often he told himself he wasn't really to blame for it, that memory — like other humiliating memories of the same kind — made him wince and flush. There had been things in his past, as in anyone's, that he recognized as genuinely bad, things his conscience ought to have tormented him over; but the memory of those bad actions never caused him anything like the suffering that these small, humiliating memories did. Those wounds never healed. And now his rejection, and the pitiful figure he must have cut in front of everyone that evening, had joined the ranks of those memories. But time and work did their part. The bitter memories were increasingly buried under the incidents of country life — petty in his eyes, but genuinely important. Every week he thought about Kitty a little less. He waited impatiently for news that she was married, or just about to be, hoping that such news would, like pulling a bad tooth, cure him completely.

Meanwhile spring arrived, beautiful and kind, without spring's usual delays and false starts — one of those rare springs where plants, animals, and people all rejoice together. This lovely spring stirred Levin up even more, and strengthened his resolve to give up his whole past and build a solitary life for himself, solid and independent. Though many of the plans he'd brought back to the country with him hadn't come to anything, his most important resolution — staying pure — had held. He was free of the shame that usually weighed on him after a lapse, and he could look anyone straight in the eye. In February he'd gotten a letter from Marya Nikolaevna telling him his brother Nikolay's health was getting worse, but that he wouldn't listen to advice; on the strength of that letter, Levin had gone to Moscow to see his brother and managed to convince him to see a doctor and go abroad to take the waters. He'd done such a good job persuading his brother, and lending him money for the trip without making him bristle, that he felt genuinely pleased with himself over it. On top of his farm work, which needed special attention that spring, and on top of his reading, Levin had started, that winter, a book on agriculture — one built around treating the character of the farm laborer as an unchangeable given of the problem, on the same footing as climate and soil, and deriving all the principles of scientific farming not just from data on soil and climate, but from data on soil, climate, and a certain fixed character of the laborer. So even in his solitude — or maybe because of it — his life felt remarkably full. Only rarely did he feel the itch to share his stray ideas with someone besides Agafea Mihalovna. And with her, in fact, he'd fall into arguments fairly often about physics, farming theory, and especially philosophy — philosophy being Agafea Mihalovna's favorite subject.

Spring took its time arriving. For the last few weeks the weather had stayed steadily clear and frosty. It thawed in the sun during the day, but at night the temperature dropped as low as seven degrees below freezing. The crust on the snow was hard enough that wagons could be driven anywhere, off the roads entirely. Easter came with the snow still down. Then, all at once, on Easter Monday, a warm wind picked up, storm clouds rolled in, and for three days and three nights warm rain poured down in sheets. On Thursday the wind died and a thick gray fog settled over the land, as if hiding whatever transformations were taking place underneath. Behind the fog came the sound of running water, the cracking and drifting of ice, the rush of muddy, foaming torrents; and the following Monday evening, the fog broke apart, the storm clouds split into little curling wisps, the sky cleared, and real spring had arrived. In the morning the sun rose bright and quickly burned off the thin layer of ice covering the water, and the warm air shimmered with steam rising from the reviving earth. The old grass looked greener, and new blades pushed up through it; the buds on the guelder-rose, the currant bushes, and the sticky birch buds swelled with sap, and a scouting bee hummed around the golden blossoms dotting the willow. Larks trilled somewhere unseen above the velvety green fields and the ice-crusted stubble; lapwings cried over the low, flooded marshland; cranes and wild geese flew high overhead, calling out their spring cries. Cattle, patchy where their new coats hadn't grown in yet, lowed in the pastures; bow-legged lambs frisked around their bleating mothers. Barefoot children ran along the drying paths, leaving their footprints behind. Peasant women chattered cheerfully by the pond as they washed linen, and axes rang out in the yard where the men repaired ploughs and harrows. Real spring had come.
